topic: Bivor: A macOS Desktop Workbench for the Pi Coding Agent

competitors.title: Bivor — the desktop workbench for the pi coding agent (official site)
key_points: Positioning tagline: 'Your coding agent deserves a workbench, not a chat box.'
Open-source macOS app for the pi coding agent; MIT licensed; Apple Silicon + Intel; ships unsigned builds (needs right-click Open or xattr -cr).
Each chat runs the pi SDK in its own isolated process — parallel tasks cannot step on each other.
Flagship features: git worktree tasks, visual harness canvas, guardrails, E2B cloud VM sandbox, checkpoints & session tree, Mission Control, scheduled tasks, subagents/browser/web.
Reads and writes the pi CLI's own session files, auth, skills, prompts and MCP config under ~/.pi/agent/ — terminal and desktop sessions interoperate, nothing locked in.
i18n: English and Simplified Chinese editions of the site.

competitors.title: GitHub — ryanlab/bivor
key_points: Described as a macOS desktop workbench built to match Codex/Claude desktop experiences, then go further with visual harness orchestration, guardrails, cloud VM sandboxes and parallel worktree tasks.
Stack: Electron 43, React 19, TypeScript, pnpm 10; each chat embeds the pi SDK AgentSessionRuntime in its own Electron utility process.
Git worktree tasks create a dedicated worktree + branch named pi/task-*; merge back from a built-in merge panel.
Guardrails: per-tool allow/ask/deny, regex rules for bash, budgets for turns/tool calls/session cost, subagent limits and a repeated-call circuit breaker, surfaced as inline approval cards.

Checkpoints: a git snapshot under refs/pi-checkpoints/ is taken before every prompt (never touches the index); restore whole workspace or individual files; forking from any message with LLM-generated summaries for abandoned branches.
Runtime presets gate capability: Daily (no coding side effects), Coding (full agent), Review (read/search only; writes/bash denied), Minimal (bash+read+edit).
Optional integrations require keys: E2B (cloud VM sandbox), Tavily (web_search), Vercel (deploy tool + ops panel), CHROME_PATH (browser binary override).
Architecture split: src/main (windows/menu/services), src/host (agent host embedding the pi SDK), src/preload (typed contextBridge), src/renderer (React 19 + zustand), src/shared/protocol.ts.
Testing story is real but niche: SDK smoke test, CDP-driven end-to-end UI run, harness E2E, CDP screenshot script (requires --remote-debugging-port=9223).
Contributing guidelines exist (CONTRIBUTING.md); README also published in Simplified Chinese.

competitors.title: GitHub — OpenPi, the closest direct alternative workbench
key_points: OpenPi is the nearest head-to-head: a desktop workbench that hosts @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent in a main-supervised sidecar instead of reimplementing the agent runtime.

Surface: session sidebar, workspace grouping, model selector, conversation stream, tool cards, token/cost metadata, command palette, customizations (extensions/skills/prompts/themes/packages), persistent Git panel, split diff viewer, PTY terminal.
Ships Homebrew cask install (brew install --cask openpi), tagged beta release automation, CHANGELOG as release-note source of truth, and star-history/social proof.
Three hard boundaries documented: renderer renders only; Electron main owns desktop authority (Zod-validated IPC); Pi SDK owns agent semantics.
Beta caveats stated up front: macOS app not notarized, Windows code signing absent, some accessibility diagnostics only warning-level.
Has an explicit ROADMAP.md and AGENTS.md and a subreddit presence (r/PiCodingAgent) — stronger community/release cadence signals than Bivor today.

competitors.title: Pi Desktop — cross-platform desktop GUI for Pi / oh-my-pi
key_points: Cross-platform counter-example: Linux AppImage, macOS DMG (Apple Silicon) and Windows installer/portable — Bivor is macOS-only in 0.1.x.

Same core mechanics as Bivor in several places: multiple workspaces each running its own agent process, Mission Control across projects, New Task into a fresh background session optionally in its own Git worktree.
Review rail with per-tool allow/deny rules (global or per workspace) and inline approvals — the same governance idea as Bivor's guardrails.
File tree, diff viewer with Commit/Push/PR actions, CodeMirror 6 editor, integrated PTY terminal, Pi package browser, usage/theme stats over 7 days to a year.
Can run either the standard Pi CLI or the compatible omp binary from oh-my-pi, reading both session stores and tagging rows when both appear.
Also ships unsigned macOS/Windows builds and documents the Gatekeeper/SmartScreen steps.

competitors.title: Armin Ronacher — 'Pi: The Minimal Agent Within OpenClaw' (why Pi is worth a GUI)
key_points: Pi's design thesis: a tiny core — the shortest system prompt of any agent he knows, four tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash).
Missing features are deliberate, not lazy: no built-in MCP support, no plan mode, no todos, no subagents in core; the philosophy is that you ask the agent to extend itself.
Extension system can persist state into sessions, which is what makes third-party assembly/orchestration layers (Bivor's harness canvas) possible.
Praises Pi as 'excellent software' — no flicker, low memory, reliable — which raises the bar for any desktop wrapper's polish.
Important for a Bivor review: the desktop layer is where opinions (guardrails, approvals, parallel worktrees) get added that Pi core deliberately refuses to ship.

competitors.title: Petronella Technology Group — Pi.dev hands-on review (compliance angle)
key_points: The security/governance case for a governable desktop layer: terminal agents have a smaller auditable attack surface, but Pi core ships with no SaaS backend and no permission system of its own.

Their three up-front decisions map directly onto Bivor features: pin the provider, contain the workspace (feature branch, no secrets, human-reviewed diff), decide session retention before the first session.
Warns that provider switching is one config edit away — i.e. an app-level guardrail that pins tools/models is a real control, not a nicety.
Advises pinning the exact npm version you validated: the compliance review is only valid for the build it was done against (directly relevant to Bivor 0.1.x wrapping a fast-moving Pi 0.99.x).
Review is dated 2026-07-23 and covers the pre-Earendil package scope (@mariozechner/*, v0.67.68) — a reminder that Pi itself has already rebranded once; verify current package scope before install.

competitors.title: ThinkRail (JetBrains) — Vibe code with pi in a lightweight, real IDE
key_points: Closest direct competitor: also a GUI for the pi coding agent, but built by JetBrains (incubator) — 499 stars, 39 forks, Apache-2.0, TypeScript, created 2026-07-08, pushed 2026-09-30 (actively maintained).
Cross-platform: macOS Apple Silicon DMG, Windows x64 zip, Linux x64 + ARM64 tarballs — directly contrasts with Bivor's macOS-only DMG.
Every working session operates on a separate Git branch merged back only after the work is finished and reviewed — same worktree-branch model as Bivor.
Also ships a CLI/browser host (`thinkrail`) alongside the desktop app, so remote/terminal workflows are first-class.
Linux builds require Ubuntu 24.04+ or glibc 2.38 with GTK/WebKitGTK — a real install constraint reviewers should mention.
Positioned on onboarding: 'New users often find themselves spending significant time learning how to navigate Pi' — accessibility, whereas Bivor positions on power/orchestration.

competitors.title: Pi Web — Web UI for the pi coding agent
key_points: 6,981 stars, 1,017 forks, MIT, TypeScript, pushed 2026-09-30 — by far the most-starred pi GUI in this comparison.
Browser-based rather than desktop: 'Local browser UI ... uses the same local configuration and session files as pi'.

Feature overlap with Bivor: session workspace (browse/resume/rename/export/delete grouped by project, running state, context usage, cost, compaction details), two branching modes (New session vs Edit from here), project file tools with Git diffs.
Zero-install interactive demo hosted on GitHub Pages — a strong answer to Bivor's unsigned-app first-launch friction.
Localized into zh-CN, ja, ru — Bivor only ships English and 简体中文.

competitors.title: PI-Desktop — Local-first AI coding agent desktop
key_points: 6,178 stars, 559 forks, LGPL-3.0, TypeScript, pushed 2026-09-30.
Architecture contrast: Electron + Rust host core + pi Agent Harness + user-installable plugins — Bivor's core is pure TypeScript/Electron with no Rust host.
Explicitly 'local-first', competing on the same desktop-pi-workbench ground as Bivor.
Docs at pi-docs.aiuo.net; permissive-ish but LGPL-3.0 vs Bivor's MIT — license matters to anyone embedding it.

competitors.title: Orca — the ADE for working with a fleet of parallel agents
key_points: 82,361 stars, 5,350 forks, MIT, TypeScript, pushed 2026-10-01 — the category leader by popularity.
Agent-agnostic: 'Run any coding agent with your own subscription', available on desktop, mobile and remote runtime.
Competes with Bivor's Mission Control/parallel-tasks story but does not require pi, so it is the substitute for users who have not committed to pi.
Scale gap is the key stat: 82,361 vs Bivor's 209 stars.

competitors.title: Paseo — Orchestrate multiple coding agents from desktop and mobile
key_points: 19,112 stars, 2,221 forks, TypeScript, pushed 2026-09-30, homepage paseo.sh.
Adds mobile orchestration Bivor lacks entirely (Bivor is macOS desktop only).
Multi-agent rather than pi-specific — the orchestration-first alternative.

competitors.title: oh-my-pi (omp.sh) — Coding agent with the IDE wired in
key_points: 33,885 stars, TypeScript, built by Stencil Labs; site omp.sh promises 'a native Rust core, with every tool tuned against real sessions'.
Windows-native ('skip the WSL') and installable via curl/brew/bun/ps1/mise — Bivor has no Windows story at all.
Appeared on HN (2026-07-21, 42 points) as 'Oh-my-pi: A coding agent with the IDE wired in'.
Self-contained harness rather than a pi front-end — an adjacent rather than substitute alternative.

competitors.title: Arbor — native desktop app for Git worktrees, terminals, and diffs
key_points: 830 stars; 'Run agentic coding workflows in a fully native desktop app for Git worktrees, terminals, and diffs'.
Same core workflow as Bivor (worktree-per-task) without the pi dependency or the harness canvas.
Useful as the 'lighter alternative' recommendation for readers overwhelmed by Bivor's surface area.

competitors.title: vibe-tree — Run AI coding agents in parallel, one git worktree each
key_points: 267 stars; desktop, web and CLI variants — the worktree-parallelism idea is now a crowded commodity.
Confirms the category norm: parallel worktree tasks (Bivor's marketing centerpiece) are table stakes in 2026, not a differentiator.

competitors.title: cc-haha — Local-first cross-platform desktop workspace
key_points: 14,794 stars; multi-agent, Git worktrees, terminals — cross-platform, unlike Bivor.
Shows how much larger the cross-platform desktop-agent-workspace audience is than the macOS-only pi-specific niche.

competitors.title: Pi-box — pi coding agent running inside a VM inside WASM inside Electron
key_points: 7 stars, TypeScript, created 2026-09-13, shown on HN 2026-09-15 (3 points).
Extreme isolation approach (VM→WASM→Electron) vs Bivor's seatbelt profiles + optional E2B cloud VM.
Illustrates the sandboxing debate around pi: pi has no built-in permission system, so every front-end solves isolation differently.

competitors.title: pz — pi coding-agent in Zig
key_points: 95 stars, MIT, Zig; 'Minimal pi coding-agent re-implementation in Zig' (created 2026-02-21).
Evidence that the pi protocol/loop is being reimplemented outside TypeScript — the ecosystem surrounding Bivor's dependency is widening.

competitors.title: pi-hosts — Give the Pi coding agent access to your servers
key_points: 46 stars, MIT; shown on HN 2026-04-29 (23 points).
Remote-execution angle adjacent to Bivor's execution worlds / E2B VM sandbox.

competitors.title: Pi: A coding agent for engineers who own their tools (Alexander Holbreich)
key_points: Third-party analysis of pi's design: 'Pi ships with exactly four tools: read, write, edit, bash. That's it. No plan mode. No sub-agents. No to-dos. No MCP. No permission popups.'
Frames the 'thick harness vs thin harness' tradeoff: 'A thick harness shrinks that model. A thin one expands it.' — the intellectual case for Bivor existing as the thick layer on a thin core.
Notes pi extensions are runtime TypeScript files with no build step, and the agent can write its own extensions.
Credits Mario Zechner (libGDX author) and states pi's core was 'deliberately kept minimal so the extension surface becomes the product'.
Also names pi's weaknesses (the review must mention these, not just Bivor's features).

competitors.title: Introducing ThinkRail (Maciej Gorywoda, JetBrains, 2026-08-19)
key_points: Publishing note: ThinkRail's announcement went out one day after Bivor's v0.1.1 — the pi-GUI race is genuinely concurrent.
Justifies the GUI category: 'Pi's strength lies in its flexibility ... This power, however, comes at a cost' with onboarding friction.
Ships CLI/browser host plus desktop; every session on a separate Git branch merged after review.

angles: 'Workbench, not a chat box' — test that claim feature by feature: what does an agent GUI add that the pi TUI cannot do (worktree parallelism, approvals, cost visibility, rollback)?

Harness orchestration is the true differentiator: Bivor is the only one of the Pi desktop apps that exposes model → system prompt → tools → extensions → skills as an editable live graph with hot re-orchestration and harness_propose self-tuning.

Guardrails as the missing Pi feature: Pi core has no permission system (per upstream README), so per-tool allow/ask/deny, bash regex rules, turn/tool/cost budgets and a loop circuit breaker are the strongest practical reason to put a GUI on top.

Checkpoints before every prompt under refs/pi-checkpoints/ (index-untouched) plus per-file restore and session-tree forking — the safety net that makes YOLO-by-default agents tolerable for real repos.

E2B cloud VM sandbox with live screen streaming and vm_gui/vm_file/vm_screenshot is an unusual capability in this category — route bash/files/GUI into a disposable desktop VM so the host machine is untouched.

Honest risk framing for a 0.1.x app: unsigned DMGs (Gatekeeper workaround required), single maintainer, last commit 2026-08-18, one open issue being 'add Windows support', and a fast-moving upstream (Pi 0.99.x, weekly releases) that can outpace the wrapper.

Category comparison as the review's spine: Bivor vs OpenPi (notarization, Homebrew, release cadence, community) vs pi-desktop.com (cross-platform, omp support) vs pi-desktop.dev (Mixture of Agents 'Pi Routing' and 'Tag Team' relay) vs the plain pi TUI.

CLI interop is the killer migration story and a genuine anti-lock-in argument: same sessions, auth, skills, prompts and MCP config under ~/.pi/agent/, so you can start in the terminal and finish in the app (or reverse) with history and checkpoints intact.

Runtime presets (Daily / Coding / Review / Minimal) reframe the app as four tools in one — the Review preset (read/search only, writes and bash denied) is a credible safe mode for audit-heavy or compliance-sensitive work.

Cost governance angle for teams: Mission Control grid showing status, current tool, subagents, tokens and cost per task, plus budgets and a scheduled-task mode (interval/daily/weekly) — directly answers 'who is burning the API budget and on what'.

Unsigned-build/security posture deserves explicit treatment: the same trust caveat appears across Bivor, OpenPi and Pi Desktop, so a review should say what to verify before installing on a work laptop (xattr -cr, source build, pinned version).

The workbench thesis: 'Your coding agent deserves a workbench, not a chat box' is Bivor's own tagline and the cleanest way to frame the whole review — pi gives a minimal harness, Bivor adds the control surface.
Feature density as the differentiator: no other pi GUI in this comparison combines worktree tasks + visual harness canvas + guardrails + E2B cloud VM + checkpoints + Mission Control in one app.
Honest maturity caveat: two releases, both unsigned, last commit 2026-08-18 — Bivor must be reviewed as pre-1.0 software, not a finished product.
The 530x star gap: Bivor (209) vs pi itself (110,766) and vs Orca (82,361) — popularity versus capability is the core tension a review should resolve rather than dodge.
macOS-only as a hard constraint: no Windows or Linux build, while ThinkRail (JetBrains) and PI-Desktop cover all three platforms.
Guardrails are genuinely additive, not redundant: pi's own README says it has no built-in permission system, so Bivor's allow/ask/deny + budgets + circuit breaker fills a documented upstream gap.
The 'same sessions as the CLI' interoperability promise is testable and concrete: ~/.pi/agent/ session JSONL files, auth.json, skills, prompts, mcp.json — start in terminal, resume in Bivor.
The concurrent-race angle: Bivor v0.1.1 (2026-08-18) and JetBrains' ThinkRail announcement (2026-08-19) landed one day apart — the pi GUI category formed in a single week of August 2026.
Preset model as the answer to complexity worry: Daily / Coding / Review / Minimal gate both tools and UI surfaces, so the harness canvas does not have to be configured on day one.
Checkpoint safety story: a git snapshot under refs/pi-checkpoints/ before every prompt, deliberately never touching the user's index, plus rollback of the whole workspace or individual files.
Steer/follow-up and mission control answer the real pain of long agent runs — Bivor is optimised for supervising many parallel agents, not for a single chat.
Cloud VM sandbox (E2B) with live screen streaming and vm_gui/vm_file/vm_screenshot is the strongest security posture among the desktop options, and is opt-in rather than mandatory.
Extension/skill management and MCP configuration are exposed as first-class UI (pi-mcp-adapter one-click install), which lowers the barrier pi is criticised for.
Self-tuning via harness_propose — the agent proposes assembly changes that require approval and hot-apply — is a rare governance pattern worth calling out as a genuinely novel feature.
Scheduled tasks (interval/daily/weekly with notifications) turn the agent into a background worker, competing with the cron-style workflows other tools push to CI.
Deployment to Vercel from the app (preview-first, secrets excluded, approval required) extends past coding into shipping — unusual scope for a pi front-end.
Code mode (code_run in node:vm with pi.bash/pi.log) lets the agent write JS instead of shell, which is a context-efficiency play worth explaining.

Where Bivor is weaker: unsigned builds and Gatekeeper friction, no mobile/remote runtime (Paseo/Orca have it), only EN/zh-CN localisation (Pi Web has four languages), and no published benchmark or user-scale data.
Browser-based alternative framing: Pi Web proves the same workflow can run with zero install and an interactive demo, so Bivor's install friction is a real tradeoff, not a necessity.
Licence comparison as a practical choice: MIT (Bivor, pi, Orca, arbor) vs Apache-2.0 (ThinkRail) vs LGPL-3.0 (PI-Desktop).
The 'thin harness, thick front-end' argument from Holbreich: a minimal core expands what you believe agents can do; Bivor is the thick layer that keeps the thin core.
Sandboxing pluralism: seatbelt (off/workspace/strict), E2B VM, or pi-box's VM-in-WASM-in-Electron — every client answers pi's missing permission model differently.

Recommendation axis for the outline's verdict: choose Bivor for macOS + maximum orchestration/guardrails; ThinkRail for cross-platform JetBrains integration; Pi Web for zero-install browser; Orca/Paseo for multi-agent fleets beyond pi.

summary: Bivor (ryanlab/bivor, 209 stars, 26 forks, MIT, TypeScript) is an open-source macOS-only Electron 43 + React 19 desktop workbench built on the pi coding agent SDK. Each chat runs the pi SDK (`AgentSessionRuntime`) inside its own isolated Electron utility process, and it reads/writes the pi CLI's own state (`~/.pi/agent/` — sessions, auth.json, skills, prompts, mcp.json), so terminal and desktop stay interchangeable. Its differentiators versus other pi GUIs are git-worktree parallel tasks (branch `pi/task-*` with a built-in merge panel), a visual harness assembly canvas with hot re-orchestration (`session.reload()`), first-class guardrails (per-tool allow/ask/deny, bash regex rules, turn/tool-call/cost budgets, subagent caps, repeated-call circuit breaker), an E2B cloud desktop VM sandbox (`vm_gui`/`vm_file`/`vm_screenshot`), per-prompt git checkpoints under `refs/pi-checkpoints/`, and a Mission Control (⌘O) grid of all live tasks. It shipped v0.1.0 on 2026-08-15 and v0.1.1 on 2026-08-18 as unsigned arm64/x64 DMGs; the last code push was 2026-08-18, so it is a young, early-stage project whose feature breadth currently outruns its release cadence. The honest review framing: Bivor is the most feature-dense pi desktop client, but it is macOS-only, unsigned, pre-1.0, and roughly 530x smaller in stars than the pi project it wraps (110,766).
